title: Aviogenex 130
summary: Aviogenex Flight 130, an international charter from Gatwick to Rijeka, took off at 16:33 GMT and suffered structural failure during landing on 23 May 1971. The Tupolev Tu-134A flipped over and caught fire. Investigation found that the crew might have suffered an optical illusion due to heavy showers and dusk that could have led them to believe the runway was closer and lower than it actually was. The crew executed an overly steep and fast descent in the last phase of final approach, causing a hard touchdown and breakage of the right wing, killing 78 out of 83 people.
probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, rain and water on runway led the crew to believe they were closer and higher from the runway than actually the case. The crew made a sharp nose-down input and reduced power to idle in the final phase, causing the aircraft to reach excessive speed and contact the runway with forces that broke the right wing.

factors.evidence: Refraction of light on the cockpit windshield caused an optical illusion that made the runway seem closer and lower (by 60 m) than it actually was.
The crew made a sharp correction applying nose-down input and reducing power to idle in the final phase of landing.
The aircraft remained above the glide path despite the crew's effort to reduce altitude by applying down elevator.
The aircraft contacted the runway at speed of 260 km/h with excessive forces (vertical load of 4g and horizontal load 1.5g) on the right landing gear that broke the right wing.

events.text: Flight 130 took off from Gatwick at 16:33 GMT, and the flight was uneventful despite poor weather conditions over Europe.
After establishing communication with Rijeka ATC, the controller warned the crew about cumulonimbus clouds above the Učka mountain range.
Approximately 3.2 km from the runway threshold, the aircraft entered torrential rain under cumulonimbus clouds.
Above the middle marker, engine power was increased and up elevator was applied, meaning the pilot initiated a go-around procedure.
The aircraft touched down hard on the runway, contacted at speed of 260 km/h with excessive forces on the right landing gear that broke the right wing.

title: Hughes Airwest 706
summary: Hughes Airwest Flight 706, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-31 flying from Los Angeles to Seattle with several intermediate stops, collided in midair with a U.S. Marine Corps F-4B Phantom II over the San Gabriel Mountains near Duarte, California, on 6 June 1971. The Phantom, returning to MCAS El Toro after diagnostic tests following an earlier radio failure, struck the DC-9; witnesses reported its right wing hit the center of the fuselage and its vertical stabilizer sliced through the cockpit. All 49 aboard the airliner and the F-4 pilot were killed, while the F-4's radar intercept officer ejected and survived. The NTSB calculated the two aircraft's closing rate at about 1000 ft/s and found that ten additional feet of clearance would have averted the collision.

tests were sufficient to determine the difficulty in locating and identifying the fighter on the radar scope

the United States Armed Forces to agree to reduce the number of military aircraft operating under visual flight rules in civilian air corridors

events.text: Flight 706 departed Los Angeles at 6:02 pm PDT, bound first for Salt Lake City, the first of five intermediate stopovers before Seattle.
Control of the flight was transferred to Los Angeles Air Route Traffic Control Center at 6:06 pm, four minutes after takeoff.
The flight passed through 12000 ft at 6:09 pm and was instructed to head 040 magnetic until receiving the Daggett VOR; its acknowledgement was the last radio transmission received from the aircraft.
The F-4B, whose radio had failed while landing at Mountain Home Air Force Base, was returning to MCAS El Toro after diagnostic tests when it approached the airliner's flight path.
Eyewitnesses reported the F-4B's right wing struck the center of the airliner's fuselage after performing a barrel roll, and its vertical stabilizer sliced through the cockpit.

The F-4's radio status at the moment of collision is not explicitly stated.

title: All Nippon Airways 58
summary: On 30 July 1971, a Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-86F Sabre jet fighter collided with All Nippon Airways Flight 58, a Boeing 727 airliner climbing to its cruising altitude of about 28000 ft. The trainee Sabre pilot was told by his instructor to break away from Flight 58, but was already too late. The leading edge of the Sabre's right wing struck the Boeing's left tailplane at an altitude of 26000 ft. The damage caused the Boeing to go out of control; it entered a steep dive and disintegrated in mid-air, killing all 162 people aboard the airliner.
probable_cause: A trainee pilot in a JASDF F-86F Sabre, unaware of the ANA aircraft, collided with the Boeing 727. Although told by his instructor to break away, the trainee pilot's avoidance was too late. The Sabre's right wing struck the Boeing's left tailplane, causing fatal structural damage.

factors.evidence: The trainee, unaware of the ANA aircraft, was told by his instructor to break away from Flight 58 as it approached.
The trainee pilot's control inputs were too late to avoid collision.
The leading edge of the Sabre's right wing struck the Boeing's left tailplane at an altitude of 26000 ft.
The damage to the Boeing's tail caused it to go out of control; it entered a steep dive and disintegrated in mid-air.

events.text: JASDF Technical Sergeant Yoshimi Ichikawa, a trainee pilot, and Captain Tamotsu Kuma, his instructor, were practicing air combat manoeuvring in their two Sabres near Morioka.
The trainee was told by his instructor to break away from Flight 58 as it approached and banked left to avoid it, but was already too late.
The leading edge of the Sabre's right wing struck the Boeing's left tailplane at an altitude of 26000 ft.
The Boeing entered a steep dive and disintegrated in mid-air, the wreckage impacting near the town of Shizukuishi in Iwate Prefecture.

title: Alaska Airlines 1866
summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 1866, a Boeing 727, crashed into a mountain near Juneau, Alaska while descending to Juneau airport on September 4, 1971. The crew received erroneous navigation radio indications that led them to believe they were closer to the airport than they actually were. The investigation found no mechanical cause for the misleading data, and the aircraft maintained proper configuration and crew qualifications throughout.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the crew's descent below safe altitude due to consistently false information from the captain's navigation radio at several points along the approach path. The specific reason for the erroneous indications could not be determined.

factors.evidence: the captain's navigation radio had apparently presented the crew with consistently false information at several points along the approach path
